result.reason: Letter A is clearer: it uses labeled sections, breaks the three portfolio actions into separate short paragraphs, and translates the jargon a non-specialist would trip on (defines duration in plain terms, explains call risk as the issuer taking the bond back early) while tying the short duration back to the account's two-year spending job. It also places the required yield-to-maturity disclosure immediately after the 3.72% figure it qualifies. Letter B compresses performance, the roll, duration, and the agency trim into dense blocks and leaves "time-weighted total return," "strategic roll," "callable agency spreads were too tight," and "duration" unexplained, and it strands the disclosure at the foot of the letter away from the number it modifies. On tone, A is plain and direct and closes with a concrete offer to walk through the rungs and maturity schedule, which fits a retired client who checks yields daily and a spouse running the budget. B drifts into corporate and mildly promotional register ("I am pleased to share," "a change that will benefit your account," "our commitment to providing high-quality service at a sustainable cost," "efficient schedule") — a fee cut needs no selling — and repeatedly says "our ladder"/"our benchmark," centering the firm over the household; it also drops the firm letterhead, date, and any invitation to follow up. B's only real edge is naming safety of principal up front, which does match the mandate, but that does not offset the denser prose, misplaced disclosure, and promotional gloss. Judgment is on clarity and tone only, not length or accuracy.
